title: Mobile SEO and Page Speed for Hotel Websites
excerpt: Mobile-first indexing and Core Web Vitals explained simply for hotel owners, with fixes for heavy galleries and booking-engine scripts and questions to ask your developer.
description: Mobile SEO for hotel websites: mobile-first indexing, Core Web Vitals in plain language, image galleries, booking scripts and PageSpeed Insights.
html:
Mobile SEO for a hotel website means making sure the mobile version of every page has the same content as the desktop version, loads quickly on an ordinary phone, and responds smoothly when guests tap. Google mainly uses the mobile version to index and rank sites, so heavy galleries and slow booking-engine scripts directly affect how you are found.

Mobile-first indexing in plain language

Google mostly looks at the mobile version of your website when deciding what your pages are about and how to rank them. This is called mobile-first indexing. In practice it means:

  • If something appears on your desktop site but not on mobile (room descriptions, policies, reviews, FAQs), Google may not take it into account.
  • If your mobile pages hide text behind tabs or "read more" buttons, that is generally fine, as long as the content is in the page.
  • If the mobile site is a separate, cut-down version, it is likely costing you.

Most modern hotel websites use a responsive design, where the same page adapts to the screen. That is the simplest setup to get right. The thing to check is that nothing important was removed from mobile layouts to make them "cleaner".

Core Web Vitals, explained simply

Core Web Vitals are three measurements Google uses to describe how a page feels to use. Google's documentation describes what counts as good for each:

MetricWhat it means for a guestGood, per Google
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)How long until the main thing on the screen, often your hero photo, has loaded2.5 seconds or less
Interaction to Next Paint (INP)How quickly the page responds when the guest taps a button, opens a menu or picks datesUnder 200 milliseconds
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)Whether things jump around while loading, so the guest taps the wrong buttonBelow 0.1

These thresholds come from Google's Core Web Vitals documentation. Page experience is one of many things Google considers. A fast page with poor content will not rank, but a slow page frustrates the guests who do arrive.

Why hotel sites are usually slow

Heavy image galleries

Hotel websites rely on photographs, and that is right. The problem is how they are delivered. Common issues:

  • Photos uploaded straight from a camera or phone, several megabytes each, and shown at full size on a small screen.
  • A homepage slider loading ten large images before the guest sees anything.
  • Galleries that load every photo at once, rather than as the guest scrolls.
  • Old image formats when newer, smaller ones such as WebP or AVIF would look the same.
  • Background videos on the homepage that start downloading immediately on mobile data.

Booking-engine and third-party scripts

The booking engine widget, chat tools, review badges, tracking pixels, social feeds and map embeds are each pieces of code from other companies. Each one adds work for the phone. A date picker that loads slowly or a chat bubble that appears late and shifts the page will show up as poor INP or CLS.

  • Load the booking widget only where it is needed, or as a button that opens the booking page.
  • Remove tools you no longer use, such as old chat widgets or retired tracking codes.
  • Replace an embedded Instagram feed with a few static photos linking to your profile.
  • Load the map only when the guest taps to view it.

How to check your site with PageSpeed Insights

PageSpeed Insights is Google's free tool for checking a page. Enter a URL and it shows two kinds of results:

  • Field data, from real Chrome users visiting your site, if Google has enough of it. This reflects actual guest experience.
  • Lab data, from a simulated test on a mobile device. This is useful for diagnosing problems, and its "opportunities" and "diagnostics" sections point to the causes.

Test your homepage, one room page, your rates or booking page and one blog or destination page. Always look at the mobile tab first. Do not chase a perfect score; focus on getting the three Core Web Vitals into the good range and on the specific problems flagged. Google Search Console also has a Core Web Vitals report that groups similar pages across your site.

A mobile SEO checklist for hotel websites

  • Every room, policy, FAQ and location detail on desktop is also on mobile.
  • Each page has its own title and description naming the property, place and room or topic.
  • Images are resized for the screen, compressed and in a modern format.
  • Gallery images below the first screen load only as the guest scrolls.
  • Image and video areas have set dimensions, so the page does not jump.
  • Only one chat or WhatsApp button, placed so it does not cover content.
  • Tap targets (buttons and links) are large enough and not crowded together.
  • Text is readable without zooming.
  • Pop-ups do not cover the main content on arrival.
  • The booking engine opens quickly and the date picker is easy to use on a phone.
  • Name, address and phone match your Google Business Profile and OTA listings on MakeMyTrip, Booking.com and Airbnb.

Speed and indexing are only part of mobile usability. To see how real guests get on, try our 30-minute mobile user test for hotel websites.

What to ask your developer

You do not need to understand the technical details to ask the right questions. Take these to your developer or agency:

  1. Is the mobile version showing all the content the desktop version has?
  2. What are our Core Web Vitals on mobile for the homepage, room pages and booking page, and which are not in the good range?
  3. Are our images resized, compressed and served in a modern format, and do galleries load lazily?
  4. Which third-party scripts load on every page, and can any be removed, delayed or loaded only where needed?
  5. Does the booking engine widget slow the page, and is there a lighter way to include it?
  6. Is anything causing the layout to shift as the page loads?
  7. Is the site using caching and a content delivery network?
  8. Can we check these numbers again after each change?

Ask for answers in writing with before-and-after PageSpeed Insights results. Our web design and development page explains how this kind of work is usually scoped, and the website UX post covers layout decisions beyond speed.

Frequently asked questions

Does page speed directly affect my hotel's Google ranking?

Page experience, including Core Web Vitals, is one of many signals Google considers, and relevant, helpful content matters more. Speed has its biggest effect on guests: a slow page means more people leave before seeing your rooms or prices. Improving speed is worthwhile for bookings even where the ranking effect is small.

My PageSpeed score is low. Should I rebuild the website?

Not necessarily. Many slow hotel sites improve substantially by compressing images, lazy-loading galleries, removing unused scripts and handling the booking widget differently. Fix those first and test again. Consider a rebuild only if the underlying platform or theme prevents those fixes, or if the site has other serious problems.

Why does PageSpeed Insights show different results each time?

Lab tests simulate a device and network, and results vary between runs. Field data, from real visitors, is more stable and reflects actual guest experience, but needs enough traffic to appear. Look at trends across several tests and the specific problems flagged, rather than one score.

Is a separate mobile website a good idea?

Generally a single responsive website, where the same pages adapt to the screen, is simpler to maintain and less likely to cause indexing problems. Separate mobile sites often leave out content or fall out of date. If you have one, check it carries all your desktop content.

Where to start

Run your homepage, one room page and your booking page through PageSpeed Insights on mobile and note which Core Web Vitals are not in the good range. Send those results and the eight questions above to your developer, starting with image sizes and unused scripts.
